planting.note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep and 8 inches apart in fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this subspecies is taller and more vigorous than typical Nectaroscordum siculum and naturalizes readily.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall, 4 inches deep in any ordinary well-drained garden soil in full sun to light partial shade. This robust subspecies grows noticeably taller and flowers more heavily than the typical form, sending up sturdy stems topped with large, drooping umbels of bell-shaped cream flowers flushed with maroon and green that smell faintly of garlic when bruised. After bloom the seed capsules turn upright and dry to a decorative silvery-tan, useful in cut arrangements. Leave foliage and seed heads in place to let the colony build by self-seeding in subsequent years.

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil in early spring (or fall in mild-winter climates); rain daisy flourishes in cool weather and declines once summer heat arrives.

directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, or in fall where winters are mild. Rain daisy carries crisp white, daisy-like flowers with a dark purple-ringed eye and a violet reverse to the petals, giving the planting a two-toned sparkle as blooms open and close with the light. Unlike many Cape daisies it tolerates slightly damper conditions and cooler temperatures, making it a good choice for cool-season bedding or wildflower mixes before summer heat sets in. Shear plants back after the first flush to encourage a second round of bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in acidic, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this is the oldest and most widely grown lithodora cultivar, prized for its long season of intensely saturated blue flowers.

directions: Plant in acidic, sharply drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; 'Heavenly Blue' is the classic lithodora selection, forming a dense, low, woody-based mat of small evergreen leaves smothered from late spring into summer in brilliant gentian-blue, five-petaled flowers. It performs best where summers stay cool and humid, as in the Pacific Northwest or coastal gardens, and resents hot, humid inland conditions and alkaline soil, which can cause rapid decline. Use it to cascade over rock walls, line pathway edges, or fill gaps in a sunny rock garden; top-dress with sulfur or an acidic mulch if soil pH drifts upward over time.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing seed onto the surface of the mix since light aids germination; transplant after frost danger passes into full sun and lean, well-drained soil.

directions: Start seed indoors under light, pressing it onto the surface rather than covering, then transplant after last frost into full sun and lean, well-drained soil. 'Silver Dust' is a compact, extra-finely dissected selection of dusty miller, forming a tidy mound of lacy, intensely silver-white foliage that stays more uniform and dwarf than seed-grown straight species plants, making it a dependable edging and container filler. It tolerates heat, drought, and coastal salt spray with ease, and its brightness makes an effective foil for deep purple, red, or blue companions in mixed plantings. Pinch off any yellow daisy-like flower stalks to keep the plant's energy focused on fresh foliage production.

planting.note: Plant rooted slips or divisions 12-18 inches apart along slope contours in spring after soil has warmed; 'Sunshine' is a selected, consistently sterile clone favored in the US for erosion-control plantings because it carries no risk of seeding into waterways.

directions: Plant rooted slips 12-18 inches apart along contour lines on slopes, ditches, or stream banks in full sun and any soil type. 'Sunshine' is a named, clonally propagated vetiver selection bred and distributed specifically for use in the United States because it reliably sets no viable seed, avoiding the naturalization concerns raised by some wild-type vetiver populations in warm, humid regions. Clumps develop the same extraordinarily deep, fibrous root system that makes the species the standard bioengineering plant for slope stabilization, while the fragrant roots can still be harvested after two to three years for sachets or distillation. Divide established clumps every few years to renew vigor and generate new planting material.

planting.note: Plant container stock or tuberous divisions after last frost in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; the white form is slower and less rampant than the common pink-flowered species.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun against a fence, arbor, or trellis after frost danger has passed. 'Album' is the pure white-flowered selection of coral vine, bearing the same airy sprays of small, heart-shaped blooms as the common pink form but in crisp, clean white, making it a softer choice for pairing with other bright-flowered vines or pastel plantings. It shares the species' vigorous climbing habit, heat tolerance, and tuberous roots that allow regrowth from the base after winter dieback in the cooler end of its range. Provide sturdy support and be prepared to prune hard each spring to manage its size.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; the white form is less commonly offered than the standard violet-purple species and grows at a similar rate.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun with strong trellis or arbor support for its heavy woody growth. 'Albiflora' is the white-flowered counterpart to the familiar violet queen's wreath, producing the same long, cascading racemes of star-shaped blooms but in clean white with pale calyces, so the persistent star-shaped calyces left behind after petal drop read as a soft, ghostly echo rather than the two-toned purple effect of the species. Like the type, it climbs by twining, tolerates drought once established, and flowers most heavily in a spring flush with lighter repeat bloom through the warm months. Reserve it for sheltered, frost-free zone 10-12 landscapes.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into wall crevices, rocky soil, or shaded borders; cold stratification over winter breaks dormancy, and this species shares the free-seeding habit of its yellow-flowered relative.

directions: Sow fresh seed in fall into gritty, well-drained soil or wall and paving crevices in partial to full shade, allowing winter cold to break dormancy before spring germination. White corydalis is a close relative of the more familiar yellow-flowered Pseudofumaria lutea, sharing its ferny, blue-green foliage and tidy mounding habit but carrying soft creamy-white, spurred flowers instead, giving a gentler, more luminous look in a shaded rock garden or wall planting. It blooms over a long season from spring into fall and self-sows modestly into suitable crevices without becoming aggressive. Once established in the thin, sharply drained soil it favors, it needs essentially no maintenance beyond the occasional removal of unwanted seedlings.
